paragraphs: Residents of neighborhoods with more trees and parks tend to report better health than residents of barer districts. It is tempting to conclude that green space improves health, and a number of researchers have argued exactly that, citing reduced stress and greater opportunity for exercise. Yet people are not assigned to neighborhoods at random. Families with higher incomes can afford to live near parks, and higher income is itself associated with better health through access to care and nutrition. A fair assessment, then, is that green space may well contribute to health, but the observed association cannot by itself show how large the contribution is. Studies that follow residents who move into greener areas for reasons unrelated to health would be more informative.
